'''Martha J. B. Thomas''' (13 March 1926 – 16 October 2006) was an American chemical engineer and analytical chemist. She is known for her work on [[phosphorus]], which made early fluorescent lighting more commercially viable by balancing the color to a natural white. Her research also scaled phosphor production to the plant level which impacted many other phosphor technologies including early [[color television]] and anything labeled "[[Phosphorescence|glow in the dark]]". Thomas was named a Fellow of the [[American Institute of Chemists]]. 

== Life and education ==
Martha Jane Bergin was born in [[West Roxbury]], [[Boston]], on 13 March 1926 to Augusta and John Bergin.<ref>{{Cite web|title=U.S., Social Security Applications and Claims Index, 1936-2007|url=https://www.ancestry.co.uk/cs/offers/join?sub=299067163049984&dbid=60901&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ancestry.co.uk%2Fdiscoveryui-content%2Fview%2F23043246%3A60901%3Ftid%3D%26pid%3D%26queryId%3Df5a0825c373745106431e145ae5af3ce%26_phsrc%3DogM91%26_phstart%3DsuccessSource&gsfn=&gsln=&h=23043246|access-date=2022-01-15|website=www.ancestry.co.uk}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=18 Oct 2006, Page 22 - The Palm Beach Post at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/227107153/?terms=martha%20bergin&match=1|access-date=2022-02-19|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Martha Thomas Obituary (2006) - Boston, West Roxbury, MA - Boston Globe |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/bostonglobe/name/martha-thomas-obituary?id=25840450 |access-date=2025-11-22 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref> As a child she attended [[Boston Latin Academy|Girls Latin School]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=18 Oct 2006, 17 - The Boston Globe at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/443754846/?terms=martha%20bergin&match=1|access-date=2022-02-19|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref> She graduated cum laude from [[Radcliffe College]] in 1945 with a Bachelor of Science degree, after which she obtained a PhD in chemistry from [[Boston University]] ([[Sigma Xi]]) in 1953, while working at [[Sylvania Electric Products]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/mothersdaughters00stan|title=Mothers and daughters of invention : notes for a revised history of technology|author=Stanley, Autumn|date=1995|publisher=Rutgers University Press|isbn=0813521971|location=New Brunswick, N.J.|oclc=31782818|url-access=registration}}</ref><ref name=":4">Martha J.B. Thomas, Society of Women Engineers records (LR001539), Box 193 Folder 12, Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, Wayne State University</ref> Later in life, she received an MBA at Boston's [[Northeastern University]] in 1983.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/11743/title/Boston-Museum-Honors-GTE-Chemist-With-1991-New-England-Inventor-Award/|title=Boston Museum Honors GTE Chemist With 1991 New England Inventor Award|website=The Scientist|access-date=2018-03-30}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Thomas began her professional career in 1945 at [[Sylvania Electric Products]], later GTE Sylvania, where she became the head of the Phosphor Research and Development Section  in 1970. During her time at Sylvania she established their first phosphor pilot plants. She was a director of technical services at GTE Electrical Products Group in [[Danvers, Massachusetts]], US, working for the company for over four decades. During that time she made "23 official improvements in lightbulbs".<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2"/>

Thomas held 22 U.S. patents and 13 foreign patents for improving lighting technology and manufacturing, covering, for example, fluorescent lamps and phosphor chemistry.<ref>{{Citation|title=Fluorescent lamp|date=1959-05-01|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US2962616A/en|accessdate=2018-03-30}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Citation|title=Process for reclaiming yttrium orthovanadate phosphors|date=1970-06-30|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US3668140A/en|accessdate=2018-03-30}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=Discharge lamp and phosphor|date=1956-03-02|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US2901647A/en|accessdate=2018-03-30}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=Flame process for manufacturing phosphors|date=1970-12-31|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/CA945358A/en|accessdate=2018-03-30}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=High pressure mercury vapor lamp|date=1956-03-02|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US2919365A/en|accessdate=2018-03-30}}</ref> One significant contribution was the development of a white phosphorus powder coating for [[Fluorescent lamp|fluorescent tubes]] creating a much more daylight-like light.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/changingourworld00hatc|title=Changing our world : true stories of women engineers|last=E.|first=Hatch, Sybil|date=2006|publisher=American Society of Civil Engineers|isbn=0784408351|location=Reston, Va.|oclc=62330858|url-access=registration}}</ref> She also developed a phosphor-based treatment that increased the brightness of mercury lamps by 10%.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ai.eecs.umich.edu/people/conway/Awards/SWE/SWE%20Nat%20Ach%20Awd%2010-06.pdf|title=The Society of Women Engineers Achievement Award Booklet}}</ref>

GTE Sylvania was a pioneer in early [[color television]] when the first commercially viable models debuted. Thomas's patent US3668140, a Process for [[Yttrium orthovanadate|Yttrium Orthovanadate]] Phosphors, showed that her research with phosphors extended beyond lightening and contributed to GTE Sylvania's 1964 color television which used an Europium Yttrium phosphor to improve the color red.<ref name=":5" />

Thomas was an adjunct professor of chemistry at [[Boston University]] between 1952 and 1970. She was also an adjunct professor at the [[University of Rhode Island]] from 1974 - 1978.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=1964-06-05 |title=SYLVANIA DEVELOPS NEW COLOR-TV TUBE (Published 1964) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/06/05/archives/sylvania-develops-new-colortv-tube.html |access-date=2025-11-22 |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards, honors and memberships ==
Thomas was an active member in the [[American Chemical Society]], holding several officer positions in her local section. She was a director of the [[American Institute of Chemists]] and published papers as a member of the [[Electrochemical Society]]. She was an active member and officer of the [[Society of Women Engineers]] (SWE), joining in 1951 during the organizations founding days. She was the Boston Section President. <ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" /> 

In 1965, Thomas was awarded the Achievement Award of the [[Society of Women Engineers]] in ''recognition of her significant contributions to the science of chemistry as an engineer, educator, and administrator, while fulfilling her duties as a wife and mother''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Award Recipients - Achievement {{!}} Society of Women Engineers |url=http://societyofwomenengineers.swe.org/news-archive/154-awards/657-past-award-recipients-achievement |access-date=2018-03-30 |website=societyofwomenengineers.swe.org}}{{Dead link|date=February 2023|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Fowler |first=Elizabeth M. |date=1965-08-04 |title=Radcliffe Girl's Success Formula; A Chemist Since '45, She Has 7 Patents and 4 Children A WOMAN CHEMIST WITH SUCCESS KEY |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1965/08/04/archives/radcliffe-girls-success-formula-a-chemist-since-45-she-has-7.html |access-date=2018-03-30 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1965-07-12|title=PEOPLE|journal=Chemical & Engineering News Archive|volume=43|issue=28|pages=118–122|doi=10.1021/cen-v043n028.p118|issn=0009-2347|doi-access=free}}</ref> 

In 1966, she received the Golden Plate Award as "Woman Engineer of the Year" in the category of Science and Exploration. Thomas is also listed in the [[American Men and Women of Science]], making the list before 1971 when it was still called American Men of Science.<ref name=":4" />

In 1969, Thomas was named a Fellow of the [[American Institute of Chemists]].<ref name=":4" />

In 1983, she was the recipient of a Distinguished Alumni Award from [[Boston University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bu.edu/cas/alumni/distinguished-alumni/distinguished-alumni-award-recipients/|title=Distinguished Alumni Award Recipients {{!}} Arts & Sciences|website=www.bu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-03-30}}</ref>

In 1991 she was named the New England Inventor by the [[Museum of Science (Boston)|Museum of Science in Boston]], an award given to individuals ''whose application of science and technology, creativity, and independent thought has positively impacted society''.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Martha Jane Bergin married George Thomas, a government scientist, at St Brigid's Church in [[Millbury, Massachusetts|Millbury]] on 29 October 1955 and they had four daughters, Augusta, Anne, Abigail and Susan.<ref name=":1" />

On retirement in 1990, the couple moved to [[Westport, Massachusetts]], and after her husband's death, Thomas moved to live with her daughter Susan's family in [[Royal Palm Beach, Florida|Royal Palm Beach]] Florida.<ref name=":2" />

Martha J.B. Thomas died at her home on 16 Oct 2006 at the age of 80. Her funeral was held at St. Mary's Church Winchester, MA.<ref name=":3" /> She was buried in [[Holyhood Cemetery]] in Brighton Massachusetts.<ref name=":1" />
